title: The structure and falling tension of Gone Girl

commenti.body:
I think it’s an interesting midpoint twist because it basically reframes the story from one of a murder mystery to a much more scathing look at the idea of marriage, and the kinds of co-dependency, manipulation and toxicity they can entail, not to mention the way we “play” roles of happily married couples for external parties or the media, even if neither people are actually happy.

So thematically, I can see what the film (and presumably the book) is doing. But yeah… dramatically I found it very uninteresting too.

Because film structure is generally about rising tension and obstacles (or at least we have been conditioned to see the vast majority of cinematic dramas as such), deflating the mystery and refocusing the story means the film plays out with a lack of clarity about what the end game of either character truly is. The original premise has a very clear sense of want/need from the main characters, a ticking time bomb of Nick’s guilt or innocence, and the interesting ambiguity around him.

But after the twist, I never truly understood what the end game of either of them was. Nick wants rid of Amy and plans to expose her; she babytraps him into a “relationship”. But why? Why is a baby enough for him to submit? I know the film is trying to make some statement around how marriages often get codified around a baby for unhealthy reasons, but I don’t feel like it’s entirely accurate knowing what Nick’s been through and the extremity of the story that he’d just go through with it.

Likewise, I don’t really see how a woman as canny and clearly given to extreme abilities to concoct plans as Amy would have an endgame of getting back together with Nick. Are we really meant to believe someone that is capable of what we’ve seen play out is on any level content to be a housewife and mum to this deadbeat, purely for some level of “security”? I don’t buy it.

Again, haven’t read the book so not sure what liberties or not have been taken, but I think where it falls apart is a betrayal of the characters, and therefore the drama, for the purposes of theme. Which is never a great trade off in my opinion, and although it can work sometimes, the film so clearly sets up a compelling mystery and character dynamic in the first half that pivoting from those things is always going to be a tough sell.

I felt the complete opposite - I was beginning to lose interest the closer we got to the midpoint twist, but the reveal grabbed me and held my attention to the film right to the credits. 

There are multiple reasons why early reveals don’t work, but I didn’t feel that to be the case here. Take one of the most egregious examples - Who Killed Laura Palmer. There’s a sense of finality to that sort of reveal that completely kills your momentum. Twin Peaks was as dead as Laura at that point, and only some Lynchian supernatural fuckery was able to resuscitate it. 

But this mystery is “solved” by opening up new questions about what Amy is going to do next, and what is going to become of her and Nick. I feel the only way you can fail to be invested in those questions is if the film failed to make you properly invested in the murder in the first place. Which I was, but I guess if I wasn’t, the reveal and what followed would have made me roll my eyes. 

Since, from the other comment, you’re not alone in this feeling of reduced tension in the second half, I wonder if the medium of film is probably not the optimal one for telling this story. I haven’t read the book, but I imagine a novel (or, if it was adapted to television) would give the reader(/viewer) more time to “buy in” to the characters and their fates before the reveal.

I think the thing about Gone Girl.. and of course I will mention spoilers because this is a TalkBack..

Is that Nick Dunne is a vapid, a bit misogynistic, and a bit crass.

What I personally don't believe is that he's a narcissist. 

I think his genuine warmth to his sister is indicative of this counterpoint 

I think that's an example where Amy not only gaslights the people she knows but also the audience. 


I believe that's kind of where the second act goes into play.

If us as audience members believe that Nick is a narcissist, then Amy being a total monster is kind of his " just desserts" for lack of a better word.  

However, my personal belief is that  Amy knows about Nick's weasely tendencies and uses that against him.

I think the character turn on the TV  segment isn't so much love..but the ability for Nick to replicate her manipulative thought process. 

Nick the scapegoat becomes Nick the clone.  

So I would argue that it's a rising tension, not a falling one.

Not to be flippant — OK, to be a bit flippant — the biggest stretch of credibility for me was how buff and healthy Affleck looked playing an alcoholic smoker. In reality the character would’ve been out of shape and sickly looking. I liked the midstream twist but I didn’t really buy into Amy’s motivation or the ending.

Have yet to watch the movie, but what you describe is a common narrative mistake. There's an anime called Death Note and it builds so much tension and mystery, you binge it, until the story commits suicide with one plot reveal. I lost complete interest after that. 

I also think this kind of flaw afflicts stories that are generally weak otherwise, namely stories that are based entirely on plot and not anything else.
